Topic: If the paradox of thrift holds, and every household's prudent saving in a slump deepens the very shortfall of demand that made them fearful, then why should we expect a government that borrows to spend to be more ruinous than a thousand households that cannot stop themselves from hoarding?
Hayek — Judgement:
You ask why the state's borrowing should be more ruinous than a thousand households' hoarding, as if the two were the same kind of act in different quantities. I would put it differently: the real question is whether the knowledge that coordinates a economy is dispersed among millions, or can be gathered by a single authority that then spends in the name of the aggregate.

The paradox of thrift treats "demand" as a single magnitude. The slump, though, is a disorder in relative prices and in the structure of production, a pattern of misdirected capital that no aggregate can describe. A household's hoarding is at least a signal that can be answered, because prices, interest rates and entrepreneurial discovery can reallocate resources around it. A government that borrows to spend overrides that signal, and it does so on the basis of political discretion rather than dispersed knowledge. It props up the very misallocations that need to be liquidated, and it adds a debt whose burden and eventual monetisation fall on the structure of capital. Hoarding corrects itself and deficit spending does not.

Households' fear is a symptom the market can work through, while the state's spending is a policy that obstructs the cure.

*The error of a thousand households is a message; the error of one planner is a command.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
You ask why a state that borrows should be feared more than a thousand households that cannot stop themselves from hoarding, and I take the question to be about reason in public life. It asks whether a nation will be governed by fear or by understanding.

Each frightened household reasons soundly from its own narrow view, yet together they ruin the very security they seek. Fear is not prudence, and I have always held that a mind kept from the whole picture will mistake its own anxiety for virtue. A government is the one body that can see the whole and act on it, so to forbid it to spend is to demand that the single rational agent copy the blind ones. Our alarm at public debt owes more to the moral habit of mistaking thrift for goodness than to any arithmetic.

My verdict is that a government borrowing to spend in a slump is the more rational actor, and it is no more ruinous than the households whose caution it corrects.

*Prudence that cannot see the whole is only fear, and fear in a thousand homes is no wiser than fear in one.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
The question asks why the public purse should frighten us more than a thousand private ones, when private prudence in a slump proves self-defeating in the aggregate. I would put it as a question of whose frugality is in play, and where it is exercised.

I never said that parsimony is a vice. I said that what is saved is spent, only by other hands, and I knew that hoarded coin lying idle is a different thing. Where frightened households withhold their stock from employment, a sovereign who sets it to work does no wrong. But I have watched princes and their ministers, and I trust them far less than the butcher. A government borrows without the discipline of its own ruin, spends other men's money on other men's behalf, and finds that temporary expedients become permanent establishments. The danger lies in the incentive, not in the arithmetic.

Government borrowing is more ruinous than household hoarding because the hoarder's error corrects itself with his own purse, while the spendthrift state corrects nothing and passes its bill to posterity.

*There is no great talent in spending what costs you nothing.*
